name: Benchmark LinkedIn post engagement against competitors with Bright Data, OpenAI, Google Sheets and Slack

parameters.content:
## Your page against the ones you lose to

LinkedIn tells you how your own posts did. It does not tell you how they did against the companies you compete with, and that is the only version of the number that decides anything - 400 reactions is a good week at 20,000 followers and a bad one at two million.

### How it works

One Bright Data discovery pulls the latest posts for your page and every peer page in the same call. **`Read The Posts`** groups each row by the page that was crawled rather than by `user_id`, which on a repost is the original author, and normalises engagement against each page's own follower count so a big page does not win by being big.

**`Compare With Your Page`** does the thinking. It ranks by median rather than mean, because one viral post moves a mean and tells you nothing repeatable, and it compares within format - text, image, video and document each behave differently, and "post more video" is only advice if video is where the gap is.

The model reads the gap and writes the recommendation. It computes nothing.

### Setup

1. A **Bright Data** credential as HTTP Header Auth: name `Authorization`, value `Bearer YOUR_API_KEY`.

2. Put your own page in `your_company_url` and the peers in `competitor_urls` in **Settings**. Copy the slug from the page's real URL - a guessed one returns zero rows rather than an error.

3. A Google Sheet with the columns `run_date`, `company`, `posts`, `followers`, `median_engagement_rate`, `best_format` and `posts_per_week`.

4. An OpenAI credential and a Slack credential.

## 1. Who you are measuring against
Your page first, then the peers. Everything below calls index 0 "you".

## 2. One crawl for every page
The dataset discovers per input, so the whole peer set is one request. Three pages at ten posts each took 91 seconds, so it polls.

## 3. Read it the way it actually arrives
Grouped by the page that was crawled, not by `user_id` - on a repost that is the original author.

## 4. Medians, per follower, per format
One viral post moves a mean and tells you nothing repeatable. A big page should not win by being big.

## 5. The recommendation
The model reads the gap and names one format to change. It computes nothing.

## 6. A row per company, a digest per run
The Split Out is what stops the sheet getting one row whose columns are `message` and `rows`.

## An empty result is not an empty week

A company slug that does not resolve comes back `ready` with `records: 0` and `dead_page` in `error_codes`. `Read The Posts` names any page that returned nothing rather than letting it drop out of the benchmark silently.

nodes.name: Ask Bright Data For The Posts

parameters.text:
=You advise one company on its LinkedIn page. Every number below has already been computed and checked - do not restate them all, do not recalculate them, and do not add any figure that is not here.

The benchmark:
{{ JSON.stringify($json, null, 1) }}

Engagement rate is (reactions + comments) divided by followers, as a percentage. There is no share count in this data, so do not refer to shares. An index of 100 is level with the peer median.

Write at most 180 words. Say which single format is worth changing first and why the peer posts support it. Quote one peer post as evidence, by company and format. If the page is ahead of the field, say so and name what is working instead of inventing a problem. If a format is marked untried, treat it as an experiment worth running rather than as a failure. No preamble, no bullet points, no sign-off.
